title: One Shelf, Many Stories
passage:
Every Tuesday after school, a small group of students at Midori Junior High met in the library. They were not there to study for a test. Instead, they had started a project called One Shelf, Many Stories. The idea came from Aya, who noticed that many students always borrowed the same popular books while other books stayed untouched for months. She wondered if those quiet books simply needed someone to introduce them. At first, the group made simple recommendation cards. Each card had a short summary, one sentence about why the book was interesting, and a small drawing. They placed the cards beside books that were rarely borrowed. During the first week, only a few students stopped to read them. The group felt a little disappointed, but the librarian told them not to give up. She suggested changing the cards every week so that students would have a reason to look again. The group then tried a new idea. Instead of writing only about the story, they connected each book to an everyday question. A book about a mountain climber had a card asking what a reader would do when facing a difficult decision alone. A science book about insects asked why tiny creatures sometimes survive where larger animals cannot. These questions made students curious. By the end of the month, the borrowing record had changed. Several books that had not been borrowed for a long time were taken home. More importantly, students began talking about the books with one another. Some even wrote their own recommendation cards and left them at the library desk. Aya realized that the project was not really about making old books popular. It was about giving people a small reason to notice something they had passed many times before. The books had always been there. What changed was the way students looked at them. The group also learned that small changes in presentation can affect attention. A bright card alone was not enough; a question that connected a book to a reader's own life worked better. By spring, students from another grade were asking how they could help. The project had begun with one shelf, but it slowly became a shared activity for the whole school.

The librarian later displayed a chart showing which books had gained new readers. The group did not treat the chart as a competition. Instead, they used it to see which kinds of questions attracted attention and which shelves still needed help. That gave them ideas for the next month.
translation:
毎週火曜日の放課後、緑中学校の少人数の生徒たちは図書館に集まっていました。テスト勉強のためではなく、『一つの棚、たくさんの物語』という活動を始めたのです。きっかけは彩でした。人気の本ばかりが借りられ、何か月も手に取られない本があることに気づき、それらは誰かが紹介してくれれば読まれるのではないかと考えました。最初は、短いあらすじ、おもしろいと思った理由、小さな絵を書いた紹介カードを作りました。しかし最初の一週間は、立ち止まる生徒はわずかでした。司書から毎週カードを替えてみるよう助言され、グループは工夫を始めます。物語の説明だけでなく、『一人で難しい決断をしなければならないとしたら？』など、日常につながる問いを添えることにしました。すると生徒たちは興味を持ち始め、長く借りられていなかった本も持ち帰られるようになりました。さらに、生徒同士で本について話し、自分で紹介カードを書く人まで現れました。彩は、この活動の本当の目的は古い本を人気にすることではなく、何度も通り過ぎていたものに気づく小さなきっかけを作ることだと理解します。本は最初からそこにあり、変わったのは見る側の視点でした。また、目立つカードだけでは十分ではなく、読者自身の生活と結びつく問いの方が注意を引くことも学びました。春には別の学年の生徒も参加を希望し、一つの棚から始まった活動は学校全体の共有活動へと広がっていきました。

後に司書は、どの本の新しい読者が増えたかを示す表も掲示しました。グループはそれを競争にはせず、どんな問いが注目を集め、どの棚にまだ工夫が必要かを見るために使いました。その結果が翌月の新しいアイデアにつながりました。
